utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel of the Prosecution. I am here together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. Later on this morning Ms. Patricia Sellers will also join the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Mr. Jones, appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. May it please Your Honour. I appear on behalf of Naser Oric, and I am joined with Jasmina Cosic, our legal assistant, and Geoffrey Roberts, our CaseMap manager. Apologies for Ms. Vidovic not attending today. She is proofing a witness is into that rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I was just hoping -- the fact that she's not having the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. Certainly not, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- as I am. All right. So can I suggest to you that any preliminaries be left till the end of this sitting so that we make sure that we finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly. I have a brief one which I can mention even as the witness is being brought in. It's simply to say that the witness who is scheduled for Wednesday we've decided to drop, and the reason the reason is that at this stage his evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, that way I don't get confused. I need to see who he is and you've got me on the wrong foot. Yes, here it is. That's number witness 42?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have the number in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it Srecko Lovicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour, yes. And, as I say, at this stage his evidence would be of a cumulative nature and so unnecessary. It's also not been easy to contact him due to his job and his location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I should say, we don't have a witness who we could at this stage arrange to give evidence in one day. Conversely, the witness who is scheduled for Monday and Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably will --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- anticipate will run on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- just to inform everybody on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. While the witness is being brought in, yesterday I made a mistake which I apologise for and I am going to rectify. When I said the transcript next to the video that we saw, video exhibit 441, the transcript I marked 441.1. It should become 441 -- P441.2, and not point 1. So please make note of that because P441.1 already existed. It was another transcript from the same video used on the previous occasion, but I was not aware of it. Thank you. Or I had forgotten it, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Apart from that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I notice that the transcript is not functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is functioning now. Mine is functioning. Can I suggest that you press the escape the escape button on your keyboard and if it was not functioning before it should, because sometimes by accident you press a button and you stop the scrolling on the screen. Oh, I see what you mean. It's not -- I see what you mean. On the laptop -- it is rolling on the laptop. It's on the main monitor that it isn't. So I don't know how that affects the transcript record. I don't think it should. Yeah, I know they are working on it. The thing is I don't think it should stop us from continuing. In any case the laptop is working and everyone has a laptop. Yes. Yeah, but the lines won't yeah, we missed a few lines, but anyway. Where is the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Mardel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Please make yourself comfortable and we are proceeding with your testimony. We are -- just for the sake of formality rather than anything else, because I know you are aware of this, remind you that you are testifying under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Mardel.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've heard that, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when we left off Dr. Mardel you were telling us how you set off for Srebrenica from Konjevic Polje on the night of Friday, the 5th of March, 1993. My question is: What had you heard, if anything, of Srebrenica when you were in Sarajevo before you even set off on this trip?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was always a great deal of concern over the enclaves and I worked and lived in Sarajevo, and at major meetings with Bosnian officials it was always -- the plight of the enclaves was always raised and it was well-known that -- to me that Srebrenica had not had any convoy or any form of assistance for several months and that convoys were unable to -- were not being allowed to enter the enclave. And a colleague of mine had actually been stuck in one of those convoys held up I think on the bridge at Zvornik, but I have no personal knowledge of the place. But it was always mentioned -- held up by disagreement from the Serb -- Bosnian Serbs to allow them to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we were looking yesterday at this book "Merry Christmas, Mr. Larry." And two of those chapters now are exhibits. In fact, I want to read a couple of sentences from an earlier chapter that isn't an exhibit. I can exhibit it if need be, but it's really just one sentence which I will put to the witness and I think that should suffice. It's from chapter 8 which deals with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I want to make sure that my colleagues agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's in chapter 8 which deals with Kamenica and there's a passage dealing with refugees leaving there in Cerska and it says: "Meanwhile countless women and children were forced to flee their homes to run in the snow to Konjevici where Serb troops pounded them again, forcing those that lived to slip and slide through the metre-high snow and the treacherous ice to join the already overcrowded, besieged and starving Srebrenica where conditions rivaled the worst conditions of the Middle Ages." And I just want to ask you if that description fits with what you were hearing of Srebrenica at the time, a place where conditions rivaled the worst conditions of the Middle Ages.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I arrived in Srebrenica, we did not have any authoritative account of conditions there; we only had Bosnian Muslim accounts transmitted through their radio or whatever. So it was -- it was complete -- relatively unknown whether the accounts were true or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay. So follow me, please, from line -- page 6, line 22 until page 7 line 22 are to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait, wait. I'm wrong. It has to be redacted from before. And the redaction must be from page 6, line 6. Page 6, line 6 with the words "the exhibit" -- "the exhibit is D224." From there right up to page 7, line 22. I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio, for pointing that out. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question was: Looking at that list of names, was that the group with travelled with you and General Morillon to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including myself, I recognise six out of the seven or eight names there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. That's fine. Thank you. If you could turn to the next page. Firstly you'll see at item 7, wounded: "The WHO representative made his way on foot to Srebrenica during the night of 5 March 1993." So that confirms, does it not, what you told us yesterday that you set off that first night, and didn't stay in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you look at item 4 on the same page it says: "Visit outline. General Morillon met Nasar" -- N-a-s-a-r, first name -- "the local commander of the entire Srebrenica pocket three times at the local command post of the school at Konjevic Polje at 2000 hours, 5 March, and at 0700 and 1100 hours, 6 March 1993." Now, the first meeting according to that was at the school in Konjevic Polje at 2000 hours on the 5th of March. Now, you told us yesterday how you were present for a meeting when you arrived in Konjevic Polje. Is that the meeting in question as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was General Morillon present at the meeting that you briefly attended?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He definitely was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was it in the school building?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know. There were tables, plenty of tables and chairs I recall. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, referring to this meeting yesterday, you said it was with -- "representatives" was the word you used. Is it right then that your recollection is that there was more than one representatives on the Bosniak side?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- you know, I would -- I can't say why I formed that opinion. I can't recall, you know, any details of -- of members -- of members present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. I want you to just bear in mind in reference to Nasar, N-a-s-a-r, in that exhibit and then we can turn to a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact I'd like to go into closed session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do that, go to closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We come now to your trip into Srebrenica. Could you please just describe for us what the journey was like after you left Konjevic Polje, how you travelled what the distance was, how long it took and details of that nature?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a motor vehicle, possibly a van, going up the road from Konjevic Polje, a very short vehicle journey, and then stopped and took a junction I think to the right, facing up a valley, and on foot through snow. It was dark. I was accompanied by three, as I recall, definitely very fit young men, all armed, who were very confident about the terrain. And I think they lived in Srebrenica. They seemed to be really keen to press on, to what I assumed was their homes. And they moved at a very fast pace and carried my bags, at least for part of -- for most of the way. There were zigzag -- there was a zigzag trail roughly that we were following up the hillside or hillsides, often, and they were cutting directly up the slope of the hill or mountainside, choosing not to go on the path to save time. And it was a fast pace and through -- consequently by leaving the path it was sometimes through deep snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Deep, how deep?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times it was over my knees. I wouldn't say it was all of that and if it had all been like that we wouldn't have made any progress, because that's very hard going, but at times it was above my knees. My trousers were -- wool trousers were soaked from the snow melting on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you described that these other young men were very fit and you were going at a very fast pace. How long did it actually take you on foot to reach Srebrenica, more or less?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: About six hours, possibly more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And at any stage were you able to estimate what distance you had covered?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A colleague of mine looked at it on the map when -- much later in Sarajevo and I remember him saying it was 30 kilometres. It was very hilly terrain, just -- it was a -- it was a significant journey and not one that I could easily understand how -- at that stage how they took wounded over there, but they clearly did. It must have been a great deal of effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as far as you understood it, that was the route from Konjevic Polje to Srebrenica? It was a well-trodden route. Maybe I can put it a different way. The route which you took was already one on which there was a rough trail marked out?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know -- I'm -- I -- it's -- corresponded to the route I took back. I don't remember the sort of details. I had to ask people on the way back. I did some of the route back on my own, but I have nothing -- no reason to believe it wasn't the usual route. They were just cutting the corners of the zigzag trails on the up and downhill slopes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was simply that, really, that there wasn't an easier route to take as far as you knew, was there?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not or we would have taken it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what sort of physical condition were you in at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt reasonably fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And had you been doing any activities which kept you fit or which adapted you or equipped you for this sort of vigorous exercise?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a keen -- I used to do a lot of outdoor walking. I used to be a climber, and it was difficult to keep fit in Sarajevo. I used to try with weights going up and down staircases or running around some of the underground and outside parts of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that even in that condition, this was an arduous journey for you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when did you arrive in Srebrenica, around what time?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 2.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how long, in fact, did you stay in Srebrenica for? And before you consult any notes, we would need to know what you're referring to, and if you can recollect without the notes that's better.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, five or six days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because we come to the usual -- yes, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What nights are those?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean -- Dr. Mardel, the practice here is that of course you can ask to refer to notes. The principle in viva voce testimony is that you do not refer to notes, but if of course you want to refresh your memory by reference to notes, we always allow witnesses to do so, with the proviso, however, that either party and also the Chamber itself can ask to have view of -- to see those notes. So do you want to see them, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, do you want to see them as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, because I'm not familiar with what particular he's brought.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are notes to refresh your memory or to -- as an aide-memoire, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are. They're a sketch of the numbers summarised from my reports and the dates put in -- put on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure it's not a prepared testimony, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's only this, Your Honour, I would prefer actually if the witness didn't refer to notes just for the -- as you said the preference is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would prefer, too. But, Mr. Jones, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'm going to put the question to him whether he prefers --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dr. Mardel, I'll be showing you exhibits referring to various matters so I hope it's not necessary to retain to every detail. Would you be happy and content for us just to continue without you actually referring to any notes?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be. The main note I had was to remind me -- myself of the dates and numbers that I'd written in my reports, like numbers of wounded, to save ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think I'm quite happy just to rely on memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's show them also to Mr. Di Fazio and we'll try to do it this way: If possible, please try to rely on your memory rather than your notes. If you need to refer to your notes, please tell us and we will let you do that without any difficulty at all. After you have finished, Mr. Di Fazio would like to have a look at them as well. And could you just for the sake of formality tell us when you prepared those notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The night before last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one-page summary, yes, I was alone in my hotel room and I just tried to summarise the page. The small notes on hotel note paper I was asked by Mr. Jones to comment on some papers and I made some brief notes so that the following day I could summarise my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you were alone when you prepared those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, Your Honour, just make one observation I -- before this witness even referred to the notes we interceded and certainly he hasn't referred to those notes yet. They haven't been part of any memory-refreshing exercise at this point. So while I appreciate Mr. Di Fazio is looking at those notes, really my preference is that those notes -- they haven't been referred to in this sitting that they really shouldn't be part of an interparty process of observation or consultation at this point. Really, they're private notes as far as I can tell of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the thing is they were in front of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: They're in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the witness. Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: They're in court with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I would like a copy of this to be made and to be provided with them, with the copy. For much of the material of course I'm not concerned -- I'm not going to be concerned about it but there are just some entries. Perhaps I could ask that Your Honours have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I strenuously object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a look and we'll decide, Mr. Jones. We'll hear submissions on it and then we'll decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't think there's much of a controversy here, but, if You Honours please, There's the large page which doesn't cause me any concern. There's this isolated which doesn't cause me any concern. There is this last page which I'm interested in. And on this -- and is attached to a cardboard cover. And this second cardboard cover with a single page, and again most of the notes don't interest me, but there is -- sorry, would you just bear with me for a moment. There is some notes on the inside of this last page that interest me and they'll be obvious to you why they should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd appreciate in having another closer look, because I couldn't imagine that actually there would be any issue of these private notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is the last one is this one? Is it this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I believe so, yes. I can't see from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I'll let Mr. Jones see it before we see it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that -- now, where are they -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can we have it back, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's simply this page which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I realise I have to show it -- I have to read it and I show it to the two colleagues. Let me see it together, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's the case of asking the witness to leave the courtroom for a while and we thrash this straight away and take a decision. Dr. Mardel, please -- you will understand. I mean procedurally we need to discuss this in your absence. So it's -- doesn't benefit anyone to have you hear to listen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I say something before I go to help clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because there is no heading to those pages. One is a list of minor discrepancies in Mr. -- in Larry Hollingworth's chapter that I was given to look through a few evenings ago. The other is a nutritional -- is some -- a list of points from a nutritional paper. And somewhere on that list is some things -- points that I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, if he's not interested in -- we will see them as well. We will call you back as soon as possible, Mr. -- Dr. Mardel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's -- what's your submission, Mr. Di Fazio, to start with? What do you want? From what I can see here, this part he hasn't referred to as yet. And the other part it seems to me that he has also not referred to as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think now that you have -- you have actually read through them, you can ask the questions that you'd like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't see why they ought to be in the records now unless there is a good reason for them to be following your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I'd like to have a copy, though, because, I mean, I haven't got an elephant's memory, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is the whole thing. This is the whole thing, because they have not been made use of by the witness although he had them in front of him. So technically speaking that the whole issue arose because Mr. Jones saw him referring to notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So at this point in time I think the proper way to go about it is to hand them back to the witness, ask him not to refer to notes as much as possible because I can't stop him from referring to notes. You know now what the contents of these two pages are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, because you have -- you have read them, just as we have. I mean, for us they are of no interest until any related matter is raised, and they can -- it can only be raised by you. If you raise issues with the witness later on related to the contents of these documents without specifically -- and we need to have these documents in the records, then we will get them in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. When you say "get them in the records," Your Honours mean -- are you talking about tendering them into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Having them brought into evidence if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if it's not necessary, I'm not interested in having more papers in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm concerned that there's a major, major procedural impropriety which is in danger of taking place here. I'll set it out very clearly Because in our submission what has just happened is wrong. Things have not gone the way they have done in the last five or ten minutes. I would correct Your Honour in terms of what you said about the witness referring to the documents or having them in front of him. He had the documents to one side in a folder. Anyways, as he drew that folder towards him, when I said please don't refer to any notes, he hadn't referred to anything, he wasn't looking in anything, and I'm sure the videotapes will bear that out. Now, in those circumstances the fact that a witness comes into court with various documents he may have one in his breast coat pocket, he may have one in his trousers. According to Mr. Di Fazio's argument any witness would have to empty his pockets because it's in court and therefore disclosable. The only basis for the Prosecution even having sighted those documents and that's why even, having had sighted documents is in my submission wrong, is if the witness wants to refresh his memory or wants to refer to the documents. The moment the issue came up I clarified with the witness that in fact he would be fine testifying without refreshing his memory, without referring to his documents. At that point, things should have stopped right there and the -- those documents shouldn't have been shown to anyone because it's not a situation justifying the Prosecution or Your Honours having sighted those notes and in fact to bend the rules to sort of enable the Prosecution to have extra material for cross-examination by looking at what is in fact privileged notes by this witness is highly improper, and, if in due course, God forbid, these notes should actually become exhibits, then certainly that's a matter which I intend to appeal and complain about fully. The fact is, if I may finish my submission, if Mr. Di Fazio would grant me that courtesy. As this witness explained he prepared these notes in his hotel room in preparation for proofing by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has every right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, imagine that I put certain questions which I am entitled to put in full confidence and full privilege to a witness. Suppose I had given him a list of questions to think about, and had jotted them down, gone to his hotel room, thought about it, written some notes down, the idea that the Prosecution should then have copies of those notes as material for cross-examination is completely improper, is completely wrong. And Mr. Di Fazio should in fact banish from his mind anything which he has seen in those notes because he shouldn't have seen them. So, Your Honour, in my submission the procedure that has been adopted of showing these notes was wrong, but that it should go no further from that, he should have his notes returned to him, he should be allowed to testify orally, as he said he is willing to do, without referring to the notes and then we can be done with. I would certainly object to Mr. Di Fazio trying to recall from memory a matter which he shouldn't have seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, the witness said that he prepared the notes in preparation of his testimony here, unless I'm -- unless I've got it wrong. Furthermore he had them ready on the witness table. They weren't in his breast pocket. So to suggest that there's been any impropriety in asking to see material that has brought into court with a witness who has said that he's created material in order to assist him with his testimony in court is the matter of the utmost concern to the Prosecution. But having said that I just fail to see what the controversy is about. I've got no objection to the witness coming back and in and not referring to his notes anymore as he has said and in fact I rather doubt I am going to have any much for him in cross-examination in any event. But there's certainly been no impropriety on the part of Prosecution and the Trial Chamber wanting to know -- wants notes if the witness himself says I've prepared them in anticipation of giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because there's a straight ambiguity in the notion of these documents being prepared for this litigation as if the witness had prepared it because he wished to submit that in evidence. What he refers to, because if he says it was in preparation for testifying, is that -- let's bear in mind this is a witness who is a doctor who is testifying about public health issues involving statistics and numbers and if he in the course of proofing felt the need to take pen to paper while he was looking at documents, then I don't see how the Prosecution says that gives them an absolute entitlement to have copies of anything which he jotted down in that context. If that were true, then we may as well go and get Mr. -- Dr. Mardel's notebook from his hotel room and make copies for the Prosecution and copies of everything which he brought to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we -- it's a storm in a teacup and we can deal with it without major ado. Let's bring the witness in again. These can be returned to him to start with, and we will solve it without any big problems. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also much depends on the question that I am going to put to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Mardel, I've given you back those aide-memoire notes that we took from you later on. My suggestion to you is that you try to do your best to rely on your memory rather than on your notes, but if you need to rely -- to refresh my -- your memory by reference to those notes, please do let us know. But then they have to be made available to everyone. That's number one. Number two, you did have them in front of you yesterday as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly had the summarising sheet. I -- whether they were enclosed in the sheaf, I wasn't really expecting to need to refer to them. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But did you refer to that sheet during yesterday's testimony at any time? I'm telling you because I was made aware yesterday that he did have a sheet of paper with notes, but because since no one raised the matter we didn't raise it ourselves. But I was made aware yesterday. I'm telling you straight and plain now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I probably -- when asked question of dates I probably would have looked at my summarising dates just because my memory for dates is not good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And can you just show it from the -- which -- and you are not interested in that, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's proceed for the time being. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for the time being, that's our decision. Later on we may come back to you on other matters, but let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if -- for the time being, Dr. Mardel, it would be good if you could actually put those papers away, perhaps in your breast pocket?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a very wise advice, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in fact, when we -- before we broke off I was simply seeking to establish how long you were in Srebrenica for. So if you can just tell us roughly about how many days?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: About five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you return to Konjevic Polje after that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So I'm going to deal with these two episodes, first your stay in Srebrenica and then your return to Konjevic Polje. First, can you give us your impressions of Srebrenica when you arrived, not necessarily that morning, but just that day and subsequent days?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, the hospital I was -- I was taken to in the night and they gave me a room in the hospital, the only lighting anywhere was a battery powering a car lamp, something the hospital -- there was an intense smell of wound infection, very obnoxious, pungent smell even in the room I was given to sleep in. I had to open the windows even though it was very cold. The town was -- the buildings were -- many people were -- many families were living together in -- in any buildings I visited. More than -- much more than the -- as many inhabitants as they could have, often with relatives or friends. Other buildings, municipal buildings, like an old school people were taking shelter in. They -- outside of Srebrenica, one region I was able to visit higher up the valley, much higher up the valley, I got given a lift in a lorry and there was very little transport available, and it was unusual to get a lift like that. I found people, again, crowded into wooden huts that they'd taken up as shelter. People were obsessed with food shortage -- with the food shortage. They had not had any aid delivered since I think November. They were generally thin. Many people I saw were, especially outside of the town I noticed some people were even physically weak even though they were parents of children, they were, you know, not in a condition to go into town, the long distance, relatively long distance to try and get food from municipal authorities or -- there was a soup kitchen that was hardly functioning and just distributing to a very small number of people in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. Firstly you referred to municipal authorities. Were you in fact aware of any such authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was clearly some functioning -- what I would call municipal authority in that they were collecting -- the air drops had started on Srebrenica I think the night I walked in. So they had been collecting the American ration packs and depositing them in a central basement, supermarket basement store. And I was able to count how many packs that they'd collected. I spoke to some local authorities for -- who were able to tell me what the -- just show me where they had distributed the aid from the convoy in November, and what little was left I think to provide support to the particularly weak. That was the purpose of the soup kitchen; it wasn't for everyone. It was for a selected, you know, sort of destitute people. But only in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say "they collected these ration packs" which had been dropped, who in fact was collecting these?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know -- and photographed children -- anyone was collecting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So are you in fact able to say whether this was something which was organised or whether it was something which was done spontaneously?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- there must have been some organisation in that they were being brought to a central point and people -- you know, I saw evidence that some people were just eating them, you know, on the road. But, you know, there must have been some cohesiveness and some social -- some social order. But I have to say a significant concern about Srebrenica, and one that I constantly heard, was that there was not a high degree of organisation. And so that would mean that people, for example, outside of the town would not be -- would not be able to access support. The refugee -- the internally displaced people that were constantly coming into the region, you know, would not be -- you know, would not easily receive care. It's not sophisticated enough, the social structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So when you referred to municipal authorities, are you referring to a civilian form of organisation just within the town itself, the town of Srebrenica, if that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Already. I wanted to return to the hospital where you arrived the first morning. Did you meet a Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: During the time you were in Srebrenica, did you see him perform operations?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you do a ward round with him?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a very long ward round.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What sort of a knowledge did he have of the case histories of the patients in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A detailed knowledge and I could ask him questions about the cases as we went through them one by one. And I made notes on -- a brief note on each patient so that afterwards I could summarise the different types of injury and conditions needing evacuation, needing medical evacuation. And he was able to give me quite detailed -- I remember discussing and asking him quite detailed questions about some individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what did you infer, if anything, from the fact that he had this detailed knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You can lead him on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I wasn't intending to put any leading question apart from this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you get an impression that he had actually operated on those patients so that they were his patients?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The surgical or the war wounded were, as far as I could see and recall, you know, must have been his patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to refer to a passage in D777, as it is now, a chapter from the Hollingworth book. It's at page 178? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The same chapter 9 of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, the one from yesterday, chapter 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is D777, page 178, and it's about the third paragraph. And I'll just read the passage. You'll see near the top it says "the next few days were dominated by the" -- page 178. Yes. "The next few days were dominated by the Simon saga," it says. If we go further down to the second paragraph, in the third sentence it's referring to Nedret Mujkanovic. His first words to Simon were: "'I'm so glad you have come. There have been so many patients. I could not do any more than I've done.' An explanation to a fellow professional, and an apology to his patients, living and dead, from a trained paediatrician who had carried out more than a thousand general operations without equipment, without drugs, without lighting, while being shelled. Nedret gave Simon a quick tour of the hospital and confirmed Simon's worst fears. There was no food, no medicine and twenty deaths a day." Now, does that fit with your understanding of what Dr. Mujkanovic had been doing in the period prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I think it's wrong about him being a trained paediatrician, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But apart from that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, before I move to another area I want to ask you whether, in the days you were in Srebrenica, did you have an opportunity to see the town itself and the buildings around the town?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you take any photographs?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have several photographs which I'm not sure -- copies will be distributed. There are I think eight of them, but as they deal with different subjects I'm going to exhibit them separately rather than as one photographic exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And for the moment -- well, we'll distribute the photographs and then I'll select the two which I want to look at now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do it whatever way you like, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, firstly, I'll just ask you just to look at all the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could look at the whole bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And tell us whether you recognise those photographs.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're all photographs I took in Srebrenica or possibly in Konjevic Polje. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Well, we'll deal with each one, one by one.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they're from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, all but two of these pictures show people, but for the moment I just want to look at the two which -- which do not show people, which show buildings. And if you could just tell us where those were taken, those pictures were taken. There's one with a minaret on the right-hand side and then one of a burnt-out building.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: One is what I recall as the town -- as the centre of town and another part -- another part of Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is going to confuse matters, Mr. Jones. Let me come to assistance. Take -- Madam Usher, please remove the photo which is at the bottom of -- on the screen. Yes. And put the other on centre. Now, this document, let's mark it straight away, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become Exhibit D779. Correct? D779.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you just tell us what that shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, because he will be using them at different times, I suppose. So let's give them separate ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 779. Could you kindly explain to us or describe to us what this photo depicts, Dr. Mardel, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in the town of Srebrenica at a junction of several streets or -- or paths. And it shows a number of buildings, some of which are completely destroyed and offer no -- offer no form of shelter or very little shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that a common or uncommon sight in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a common sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then the next photograph which would be D780.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, but back the other photo I asked you to remove earlier on, please. Now, this photo which shows a minaret on the right-hand side is being marked as Defence Exhibit D780, D780. And once more, Dr. Mardel, I mean, I'll ask you to describe what it depicts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's looking down a high street. There's an abandoned or destroyed car and there's signs of some vehicle tracks in the road, people walking, and most of the houses on one side of the street are badly, badly damaged, again offering no effective shelter from the heavy snow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, I'm finished with those two photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's referring with the previous photo, the one which was 779, if you can put it back. Let's -- looking at the it again, the building in the -- at the -- on the left of the photo, that's not the main mosque in Srebrenica, with the Domavija Hotel in the back, maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't recall. It looks sort of Ecclesiastical. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jones, for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Srebrenica, did you assess the public health situation in the town?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown D232, and -- Defence Exhibit D232, and we looked at this briefly yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, are you in fact the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One preliminary matter. The date on the front page is written as 23/2/93. Is that in fact accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been a mistake and another thing I should point out, the distribution to those agencies, this is -- later given to them in response to a request. The main document was not written, obviously, with them in mind. It was for general distribution to all agencies, and particularly my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Aside from that error in the date -- well, firstly, do you know in fact you prepared this report?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared the report with -- about a week -- you know, within the days or week following my departure from Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. So apart from the date, can you otherwise confirm the contents of this report as being accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this document has two parts, firstly details of medical facilities and conditions in Srebrenica, which is pages 1 to 4, and then from pages 4 to 8, summary of visit to Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica 5th March to 12th March, 1993, by Dr. Simon Mardel. I'm actually going to start with the second section, this summary of your visit. This report describes the situation as you found it in Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje in that period?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I want to ask you about a number of the public health issues which are set out in this document. First the mortality rates, and it's at page 5. You see the heading "mortality." I'm just going to read that paragraph. "I was told that 20 to 30 people were dying each day from illness related to malnutrition. I looked at two of the six cemeteries in Srebrenica and found several fresh graves in each, supporting these figures. Two young patients in hospital had severe pneumonia with no underlying cause except malnutrition. The local doctors described seeing cases of typhoid with confusion and chest infection as frequent complications. Speaking to travellers from neighbouring villages, I ascertained that within the last few weeks six people of different age groups had died with dysentery in a village because Brezovica, whose population was about 500. They did not know if these cases had fever. There were reports of large numbers of lice infestation in the villages." Do you see there, number of items, 20 to 30 people dying a day from illness related to malnutrition, young people with severe pneumonia, reported deaths from dysentery. Would it be fair to say that death was all around in Srebrenica in this period of March 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There were a lot of things which could kill you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would that be much more so even than in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just broadly, though, those figures would -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in this situation would you make the same assumptions about causes of death that you would see in the UK in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's more -- one would take into account more of the contributing factors. For example, if these young patients -- and by that, when I say young patients, they would not have been children, these were young adults, otherwise I would have said children, and it's unusual to get young adults with pneumonia without having something that makes them more vulnerable to pneumonia or a very bad pathogen like TB. In this case, I think all of the -- these pneumonias were due to the underlying nutritional status.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to ask you this: Obviously Srebrenica was a war zone. Were the conditions that you observed in Srebrenica simply those that you would expect in any war zone or were they better or worse? How did they compare?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two aspects. Firstly -- were different. Firstly, there's nowhere else they could go to. Where I worked in other war -- war-affected countries like Afghanistan and refugees from Ethiopia, you know, when conditions became intolerable, they could move, they would move. People in Srebrenica didn't have any choice, like to move to another town. Many of them had already done that. They'd been internally displaced people from one town to another, and Srebrenica seemed to be the end of the line. There was no easy way out of Srebrenica that people could walk, for example, with their families. So I found that highly unusual to have a population that seemed to be facing a military onslaught but with no refuge. The second thing is the conditions were of a besieged enclave, and this is -- that is not a common situation, to have a huge number of people in a pocket facing extremes of weather and injury and illness with no -- you know, with no supplies at that stage of food or medical aid or even -- even hygiene, you know, difficulties of soap, washing. And I would also say that those conditions clearly deteriorated further after I left when the water supply to the city was cut off some weeks after I left. I say "city," town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that illness related to malnutrition was a common cause of death at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: People in these situations, we deal with reports which we have to try and establish the truth. Obviously, the risk of exaggeration from the local sources has to be taken into account. And I felt that, given that I was seeing pneumonia and, you know, degree of -- the degree of malnutrition I was seeing in some cases, I felt it did -- it did support that claim if -- although I can't validate the extent of it, whether they were all due to malnutrition, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, from what you saw, was it common or uncommon to see people who looked emaciated in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I often saw that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how common was it to see people who looked exhausted?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- that was also -- you know, I commonly came across people like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you would see someone with sunken eyes, what, if anything, is that symptomatic of?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be prolonged malnutrition because the fat tissue behind the eyes is consumed by the body over prolonged starvation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sometimes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And dehydration can also cause it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was it rare or common to see people around Srebrenica who had sunken eyes?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I think that my impression of nutritional status was, you know -- I even measured arm circumferences or, you know, just -- you can't help but seeing -- noticing someone's face overall as being thin and pinched. People are wearing as much clothing as they have available, so the sunken eyes may be one feature. I wouldn't say that it was -- it's the thing I would look for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. You've mentioned arm circumference. I would ask if you could look at a couple more photographs, and I'd start with the one -- the single one of a man on a bed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, for the record, this photo which shows a man on a bed is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D781.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the arms on that gentleman, how would you describe those? Would you describe them as being symptomatic of anything?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's lost a large amount of the normal muscle mass that's best and most commonly measured in the upper -- in the mid-arm where the biceps and triceps are. So he's quite obviously very thin, due to both fat and muscle loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if we look at his right thigh, is there any comment you could make about that appearance?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: His right thigh has what we can see in the picture as a dressing extending up to it. I think there's an impression of a bony prominence of the pelvis which would also indicate that he's utilised all -- he's broken down all his muscle, a great deal of his muscle mass.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you recall where you saw that person and where you took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would almost certainly have been in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the next photograph is of three men in a truck. And I'm not sure if -- well, perhaps you can help us with whether in fact they're all living or not and with what that picture shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this photo which the witness is now being shown of three gentlemen in a truck, Vlasenica 109, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D782.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a trailer being towed by a very simple tractor device. I think they just have one wheel and large handle bars. So they were sometimes used to transport our people. So it's not a truck as such. They're quite specific to that region. I -- we saw a lot of these one-wheeled tractor devices that were very -- that could go over difficult ground. And in this case they've attached a trailer to it. There's three patients on -- is there any -- anything specifically you want me to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just this: Was this sort of a scene common or uncommon in Srebrenica in the time you were, people who appeared to be in this sort of condition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't often see this form of transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not the transport so much as the people.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it was common?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could move more rapidly on this, Mr. Jones, because I think these are things that are not really contested by the Prosecution, I would imagine. And we have already indicated to you that we have heard a lot of evidence on the circumstances of the people in Srebrenica. But please feel free to ask any questions that you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to -- to explain that it's also -- goes to the issue of what inferences one would draw if one sees someone who looks emaciated and unwell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's really on that issue. I trust Your Honours will see the relevance, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, finally -- if we can have an exhibit number for the woman on the sled, I take it that would be D783.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you describe for us briefly what that picture shows and what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall this being a man, and he had -- I think he's been injured and this was their only form of transporting him towards the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this photo which is now being shown to the witness, showing a man and not a woman, being dragged or transported over the snow is being marked as Defence Exhibit D783.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we've seen in D232, the exhibit, and you've testified about young patients in the hospital who had severe pneumonia with no visible cause except for malnutrition. That's the quote from page 5, D232. I want to ask you this: Is the risk of death and pneumonia exacerbated by malnutrition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it common for the person, the patient to slip in and out of consciousness?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a very late stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But that's a symptom of pneumonia, slipping in and out of consciousness?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not specific to pneumonia and if you're -- before dying of pneumonia, you would lose consciousness usually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a grace from God, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right, yes, I imagine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A grace from God.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, tuberculosis and I'm going to go through something of a list of public health concerns. Was tuberculosis also a public health concern in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was of concern to my health organisation that -- always to be on -- aware of the risk of TB. It's a hard diagnosis to make in this condition and we were very concerned about its possible appearance and potential for spread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient to you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I'm told that because of redactions the break has to be of 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I did ask if we could start without the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I'm addressing you straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because I feel in need of some guidance from the Chamber in the following respect. Before the break Your Honour indicated that I should -- I could move rapidly on these areas because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have a -- there's a very precise reason why I'm dwelling on this because there's been a lot of evidence on the circumstances of the people in Srebrenica. Now, Your Honour, if it's not contested that if -- if the accused or another person were to see someone who was pale, emaciated, fever, with festering wounds, it's conceded that that wouldn't provide notice of mistreatment, which is an issue obviously in this case, and which is what I'm driving at, obviously, with some of these questions. If that's conceded or if the Chamber considers that that's a point I don't need to pursue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, that point we definitely would not give you any suggestions not to pursue. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that's definitely --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why I'm curious as to why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, wait. No, because if the reason of the questions was to prove that in Srebrenica at the time there was famine, there was disease, there was, as it has been described, hell on earth, that you don't need to pursue because -- but feel free to if you want to. But in the Trial Chamber's opinion we have already told you that we are satisfied that there has been a lot of evidence already -- plus photos, plus films, videos --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- showing what condition the people were living in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's simply why I'm puzzled because I wanted -- also it follows from the fact that if it were hell on earth, the argument which I've suggested might be conceded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that you will realise we cannot concede anything on. That's a conclusion which you need to draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then -- there you are free to ask any questions and elicit that conclusion from the witness if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's important that I raise it so that you realise that the questions I was requesting this morning were in time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, at no time we wanted to curtail on -- it's a question of -- now, if you were in agreement that for the purpose of what you are trying to seek you didn't need to go into further detail, you were free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. There's another issue as well which is, the evidence I'm eliciting is relevant to causes of death of persons in Srebrenica and of course when it comes to victims mentioned in the indictment I certainly made submissions in the past that one couldn't assume that anyone who died had been murdered, and obviously I'm eliciting evidence from this witness which points to that issue. So I trust those points are taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Eventually those will become submissions, obviously -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I trust why the Trial Chamber understands why I'm asking those questions. I would be troubled if your Trial Chamber hadn't appreciated that that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes it clear. At least we can read your mind better. Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have nothing to add to this discussion. Just on another issue, I spoke to Mr. Jones just before -- just after the break and he informed me he's got about an hour, an hour and a half I think it was, Mr. Jones' estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another hour and a half more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If so, that would take us to 12.30, maximum, and that's the break. That's going to leave me 45 minutes. Now, I may be able to finish and so on -- I may be able to finish at that time but -- and you know that Dr. Mardel, I think, has a commitment or is anxious to complete his evidence today. Now, I don't want to -- I mean, I'll do my level best to finish, but I just alert the -- alert everyone to that danger and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If we don't finish, he will -- we'll have to find a solution to that. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I'll be as accommodating as I can and, as I said, I'll do my best. But I just raise -- flag that danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Jones and Mr. Di Fazio, I think you need to cooperate amongst you, try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just two observations, Your Honour. Obviously, we lost a lot of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but what can you do about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's just to explain why if there's any appearance of me overrunning, it's partly due to that. But also my learned friend indicated that I could lead on a lot of these issues, and so I probably will be taking that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think I also gave you that suggestion earlier on in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this is not someone who is really tied to -- to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to the events related to the accused as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'll lead on the public health issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then I won't lead on some other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, in fact, if you can present these health issues to him as proposed facts to which you would either -- you would need to answer yes or no only, I think we can get ahead much faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I'll explain that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'll explain to him as well, actually. I will put him on notice that if he doesn't speed up with his answers, he may end up having to return on Monday. And that I think will --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Provided he's not under the impression that he's to blame. I think he's given quite concise answers today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I will try to cut him down even further, you know? I don't know. He disappeared. I hope he didn't go on another mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Mardel, we are going to proceed and we will try to accelerate the rate of the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. We need your cooperation, however, and your cooperation would consist in trying to give more concise and to-the-point answers. I'm not criticising you, you know, please don't -- but the two lawyers will be doing their part and you will also need to do your part. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise you would have to stay here over the weekend or return on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. Which we are trying to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Mardel. In that spirit, I'm going to put questions, leading questions, put to which you can give a yes or no answer, but if you feel the need to elaborate, then please do so, just dealing with the public health issues. Earlier in your testimony you described the population of Srebrenica being exposed to extremes of weather. Is extreme cold also a health risk?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it extremely cold when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did ice in fact even pose a hazard?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, slipping, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Does an unclean water supply create additional health risks?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I still have to go slowly probably for the interpreters. Diarrhoea, was that also a menace to public health in Srebrenica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was extremely common and I saw firsthand evidence of just how common it was in groups of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can diarrhoea be fatal if someone is already compromised by another illness?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, especially in the young or elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And does the stress of living under siege and with shelling have an impact on public health, in particular in terms of a breakdown of hygiene and other habits?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People can't secure clean sources of water or make proper use of latrine areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If people are chronically weak and lethargic, is that a symptom of chronic malnutrition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask you to look at a new exhibit. It's an article from the Daily Express, 15th of March, 1993. And you may recall even without seeing it -- did you bring that article with you to The Hague as part of your collection of documents?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this article from the Daily Express deals with your visit to Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje. There's actually one specific part I want to deal with right now, which is where you see the heading "scouring." And it's the second paragraph. "I saw a 30-year-old man collapse dead as he was looking for US aid parachutes," he said. This is referring to you. "Then you were reduced to eating a crude bread made of corn cob cores mixed with tree buds. The primitive nutrition had killed some people." Now, is it in fact highly uncommon for a young man to drop dead for no apparent cause?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember being concerned and seeing the body. I was in the hospital when he was brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what could be a cause of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- there's a number of possible causes. They're all very speculative. Could have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if they are speculative, are we interested in them, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I can put it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have had to deal with in my career young men playing football and dropping dead and the result of the autopsy is -- still lead you no --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me just ask this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Dr. Mardel knows exactly what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would either scurvy and/or malnutrition contribute to that sort of a risk, sudden death?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, and that did occur to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This would become D784.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, still on that article, we don't need it in front of you, it's reported there that eating these crude this crude, improvised bread had killed some people. Is it right that that's at least what you were told, that this improvised bread had actually led to indigestion which had been fatal?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
