utterances.text: I was told it was causing them problems, but it's not something we're used to seeing, people eating pulp -- ground-down wood fibre or paper fibre, cellulose, pure cellulose. This is not a normal nutrition source. They were making their food resemble a substantial mix to make a kind of bread, grossly diluting what nutritional source they had with this. And this is not a safe -- I don't think this is a safe -- not a proper food source.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that eating berries from the woods, if you don't know which ones to eat, can cause hallucinations and other mental health problems?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible -- that's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the term multifactorial applied to cause of death or loss of life?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That describes, does it not, the fact that someone's death might be caused by a whole variety of causes?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Contributory factors, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you heard that someone had died in Srebrenica in March 1993, could that indeed be from a large number of contributory causes?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There may be a primary cause of death caused by -- led up to by something else, led up to by something else, and then on top of that contributing factors. That's how we tend -- that's how we use death certificates, for example, that's how we complete them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if someone had an untreated war wound, could that be a contributory factor in causing death?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's a reference in D232 I believe, to osteomyelitis?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what that is?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an infection in the bone and in this environment it was usually a complication from war wounds, shrapnel or bullet wounds. And infection in the bone is very difficult to eradicate and leads to chronic infection which places a great burden on the individual's immune system and nutritional status. And so they run down -- they get rundown by it in every sense and it poses a risk to life in the long term.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in the hospital, it's noted in D232, you saw 20 cases. What sort of a number is that to find, a small, medium, large number?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what does that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indicates severe wounds combined with inadequate surgery or inadequate conditions for surgery and contributed to by also a lack of antibiotics, disinfectant, hospital hygiene, operating hygiene, the physical requirements for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I think it's true to say, isn't it, that there wasn't any penicillin in the hospital when you were there?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just on the issue of malnutrition --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I will continue to lead on these issues just to make progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In D232 there's a reference to the fact that some people in villages slaughtered -- had slaughtered animals because of diminished food stocks. Now, isn't it right that, in fact, if there's meat on the market, that's not a good sign; in fact, it's an early warning sign of a famine?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In nutritional surveys it's a standard warning sign when there is a glut or a large amount of meat appears and the price of meat is cheap, as people slaughter their animals because they have no food. So they sacrifice, for example, a constant yield of milk from a cow; they have to abandon that, and slaughter the animal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about scabies and lice. Scabies and lice infestation was rife in Srebrenica, was it not, when you were there?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And scabies is a parasite, is it not, which leaves the person suffering from it to scratch and can lead to skin defects, even bleeding. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And indeed, can it lead to secondary infections such as rheumatic heart disease?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It leads to -- it very commonly leads to skin infection and persistent infections of one kind of infection can cause the rheumatic heart disease. It wouldn't be the commonest complication, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can that be fatal?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's also a reference - and I'm still with D232, but in the interests of making progress I won't refer to chapter and verse - to large skin defects and to carbuncles. Now, is it common to come across those defects in a developed country?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a previously healthy individual, they're not common. We tend to look for an underlying -- we often associate with an underlying immune problem or diabetes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Whereas in Srebrenica was that fairly common?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could that lead to some facial deformity on the face of the sufferer?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Carbuncles were among the conditions specifically mentioned to me in a list of conditions by the local doctors in their clinics. They occur on facial -- on hair -- on hair-bearing areas of skin, not typically the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But it could be on the face if there's hair. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be on the face or scalp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, there's also a reference, and it's page 2, third paragraph 2, "chronically discharging, smelly, infected wounds." That's something you came across?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what sort of appearance does that -- does that take?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people normally try and put a bandage or dressing to soak up the discharging material and -- or try and protect the wound. The dressings were always very dirty and soiled and insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Weren't they in fact reusing bandages in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- they were boiling them, drying them, and reusing them, but the discolouration produced by the -- by some bacteria, it turned them green.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, is it not also true that anaemia was common and the that sort of readings which you were told about were extremely low readings were grammes of haemoglobin for 100 millilitres of blood?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's very low.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And anaemia causes people to look pale and drawn and tired?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pallor is the distinctive feature, pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally a few other matters, and this is on the same document: "Some people admitted to symptoms of night blindness, and many patients had mouth ulcers." Just dealing with mouth ulcers, can that lead to a discharge of blood from the mouth in a serious case?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They can get cracks at the side of the mouth because the rate of new skin formation when there is nutritional deficiency is impeded. So areas of the body that are prone to constant stress do sometimes break down and you can get cracks and fissures and inflammation. So it's a sign of -- it can be a sign of nutritional deficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say in Srebrenica in March 1993, and certainly -- let's just deal with the hospital. And the hospital at any rate, there were many people who looked extremely unwell and had all sorts of wounds and injuries and infections visible on their body?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then outside the hospital within Srebrenica generally, is it also true that there were many people who again were of a very miserable appearance?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miserable and weak. And I should add that anaemia causes patients to be weak and complain of weakness. It's not something you kind of see, but, yes, it is one of the features.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to Dr. Mujkanovic briefly, on D232 -- and perhaps it would be useful if the witness could see it. It's the first page. Just if you can help us with one matter. It says there in the second full paragraph. "There is one surgeon Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic, he has general surgery experience, but no previous orthopaedic experience. He has been doing all the surgical work in the hospital and appears to have" - it says "burn out," but - "burnt out and now spends much of his time attending other matters in the town." Now, firstly, is that correct? Do you recall reporting that Mujkanovic had done all of the surgical work but he appeared to have burnt out?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, as a doctor who's worked in war zones, is that something you have an understanding of or an explanation for?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can -- it's completely anticipated for someone of that relatively junior experience to be responsible solely for all of that -- all those -- all that surgery, all of that wounded and in those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Without anaesthetics and ... I want to draw your attention to the remark which appears there. "Before being critical we should ask ourselves how we would cope with those conditions." Do you endorse that remark?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the situation which you've described in terms of public health, did you get a sense how the local population saw the prospects for the future, for their future?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- they were -- I was constantly aware and being told, and it was obvious, they were very frightened over their future. As -- as -- where could they possibly -- how could they escape from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you get a sense how, if at all, any defence of the town or the enclave of Srebrenica was organised, or who was involved in the defence? How would you characterise that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my job to look at those matters, but I formed a general impression that it would just be a matter of time before, you know, the enclave would -- would be overrun.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What in fact I was getting at is: Was there, as far as you are aware, either a professional army on the ground or fighters or men with weapons? What -- how would you categorise what you understood to be the defence of the enclave, if there was one?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impression that -- that is most distinctive in my mind was -- was it was the exception, like the three young men that escorted me into Srebrenica, they were the exception. They were fit and they were armed and they had a uniform. And I -- I obviously took a personal interest in my safety, so I was gauging people who were with me and -- when I was travelling. I would have been gauging their capability to be aware and do the right thing and make sure I was safe. And that was the only -- you know, that stood out in my memory as the only -- you know, as distinctive. It was unusual to see that. I didn't see the usual -- usual impression was of people doing -- forced to do what they could do to defend themselves because what other option do they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as for those three men in uniform, firstly, I mean, were they all in precisely the same uniform or were they in different uniforms and what sort of a uniform was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I met them later and was able to take a photograph of them, so my memory is refreshed by that. But it was trousers and smock or top, and I would have been aware that they must have had reasonable -- good footwear to do that journey safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in the five days you were in Srebrenica, you saw those three men with that equipment and no one else?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stood out in my memory. I do remember being appalled to see people with poor footwear in those conditions who were, you know - for want of a better word - defending the enclave and carrying some, you know, carrying some weapons. But I had problems, you know, I have problems sort of referring to these people as fighters and just defending, you know, the enclave. That was the impression I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, there are a couple of final public health matters which I, in fact, still need to deal with. First of all, did you also observe in the hospital decubitus ulcers, in other words bed sores, which -- being indicative of a very poor condition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Decubitus ulcers, yes, bed sores.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's also a reference to gas gangrene. Can you explain just a little bit about whether you observed that and what that indicates?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't observe gas gangrene myself, but they reported seeing and experiencing a lot of cases and I have no doubt that they were correct. And it's seeing the inevitable consequences of that; all patients will die in those conditions if they've got gas gangrene. There could be no survival from that unless surgery is effective in removing all dead tissue, and that is why a nurse with no operating experience ends up doing amputations and so on after months of seeing those things and with no effective anaesthetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And are the guidelines in fact for within what time period surgery needs to be carried out on someone with a war wound to prevent gangrene setting in?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule of thumb, we want -- we want to get a wound cleaned, you know, within six hours. If not, then they're in a higher risk and we have to take additional measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So as a matter of public health, if someone has stepped on a landmine or been shot or had a serious shrapnel injury, you need to get them to a hospital in a very short space of time?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally, enterocolitis, was that also observed and is that also a thing which can result in death?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It -- it's diarrhoea with blood in it. It doesn't usually cause death, but it could be a contributing factor. But in the young and elderly it could cause death. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'll just read into the record D232, page 2, the bottom, and this is your report: "In discussions I had with the doctors they described seeing the following cases most commonly: Malnutrition, scabies, anaemia, pneumonia, hepatitis A, and enterocolitis. They described cases of vitamin deficiency with symptoms and signs, including angular stomatitis, swollen gums, xerophthalmia and rickets."

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You found that. Now, you gave evidence about your visits to -- if not villages, certainly an area south of Srebrenica. And you say, and this is again in your report: "Apart from one industrial region close to Srebrenica I was not able to visit any of the outlying villages because of difficulty in access caused by the deep snow." Now, you told us at the time you were fit. Was this a problem that you faced or were outlying villages simply not accessible because of snow at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Movement to those regions was difficult. The only region -- I wanted to visit areas outside of town to make as complete an assessment as possible. They're more vulnerable, potentially more vulnerable, or they may be surviving perhaps better. I wanted to make an assessment, but I was -- snow was deep and, you know, it was difficult to do that. So I -- I took one -- this one place I was able to get to along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your report also refers to travel to Zepa. Can you just tell us -- I believe you had a conversation with a young man about travelling to Zepa and what his situation was.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interviewed people about their food sources. I spent time with families talking in detail as to how they got food. One large family, the father of the family would walk through a perilous route in deep snow. And he showed me snowshoes that he had manufactured himself so that he could walk across the deep snow. And I took a particular interest in the route because I -- I had a -- in case I -- if I had to leave and I could perhaps take that as an optional route. So I -- he described to me in detail the route and it would have been difficult and at night, but -- and not many people could do that journey, of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Excuse me if a moment, Your Honours. My screen has locked, so I need to unlock it so I can see the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need any technical assistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right? Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The wonders of technology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, but if you do need any technical assistance, then please let me know because otherwise we will have to wait for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. So it wouldn't be true to say that Srebrenica and Zepa were part of an easily contiguous territory with movements between the two -- with unhindered movement between the two?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, and this was a -- you know, I felt that was an exceptional route and not one -- he had relatives in Zepa, which itself had nutritional problems, but they would give him a sack of food when he made that journey, something like a monthly -- every two weeks or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I believe his sister had been killed looking for food. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He described one night they were stealing food from farms and his sister was shot at, by him --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not by him --

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, by his side, shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally a question on lice infestation. Is it correct that typhus can be carried by lice and is also potentially life-threatening?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, as an expert in public health and nutrition, can you comment on the effect of malnutrition and even starvation on people's ability to make rational decisions.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would compromise -- it's likely to compromise fine design-making and learning. Overall, people may still carry out and perform essential tasks, but, you know, judgements may be impaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were present in Tuzla, were you not, when a convoy arrived with people from Srebrenica? If you can respond to that and then I'll put another question?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was that experience or anything which you gathered from that experience, or what had occurred, did that cause you to reflect on this matter of people taking rational decisions in a crisis?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I met the convoy of -- the first convoy of people transported out of Srebrenica. And they were crushed into open trucks, standing in the back of trucks. I remember a child's arm, you know, in the air with rigour mortis, a dead child sticking out of the back. And when the trucks were unloaded there were a number of -- there were a number of asphyxiated children. They have very ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we won't dwell on that subject, and if you need a moment -- it was really to ask you this: Did that experience lead you to any conclusions about crowd behaviour in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They must have been absolutely desperate to get out. And I understood that -- I looked into it as carefully as I could. I understood that more people tried to climb in to the lorries. And even at the final checkpoint or further down the road, families even threw their -- you know, threw their children on to the lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We're going to come back to that with an exhibit, but we're going to move on to a different area now. While you were in Srebrenica, were you able to communicate with the outside world?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through the -- through an amateur radio link to another amateur radio in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall who was manning the radio?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two young twins from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you still have the photographs next to you? Can you see whether there's a picture of those twins there?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. I recall it, yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And perhaps we should premark the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We need to do that straight away. So this photo which shows two gentlemen, one of whom is -- seems to be operating the Morse code transmitting device is being marked as Defence Exhibit D785.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dr. Mardel, can you just describe for us a little bit firstly who these youngsters were, if I can describe them as that, and how the communication worked, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war they were amateur radio enthusiasts and they continually manned this radio room, and it was the only link with the outside world until the UN later arrived and set up more sophisticated communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, was this room guarded?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the room every -- every day to report and keep in touch. It was my only way of keeping in touch and the UNHCR had someone stationed in Tuzla at the other end, so to speak, at the other radio. So I had an effective way of communicating --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll put it this way. I mean, we -- first of all, I take it you accept they're in civilian clothes, these two?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there any military presence around this radio? Was there a uniformed guard with a rifle or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. It's possible. It's -- it was all a bit -- it wasn't highly organised. It's possible, but it was -- I just came and went and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't -- I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you have to seek any permission to use this radio?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was the equipment sophisticated?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's just an amateur radio short-wave radio set. I would not -- you know, if -- most people would not now call that -- would not have called that then sophisticated, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall how it was powered?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was powered by car or vehicle batteries, and I asked how they were able to charge them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And their answer?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used fuel that they drained from electricity substations -- there's a mineral oil or something that is used to cool the transformers, and they drained quantities of this oil to fuel engines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you recall whether this was a secure line or where the Serbs were able to intercept?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They constantly found the frequency -- they constantly interrupted us and would jam or shout abuse or both. And then it took time, therefore, every 30 seconds or minute to then -- the twins would find another frequency that was prearranged and then would continue the conversation until that was jammed. So I spent a lot of time just to transmit quite short messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, skipping ahead slightly. You used the radio in Konjevic Polje as well, didn't you, upon your return?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember who manned that radio?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I distinctly remember it was a wounded young man who, you know, perhaps because of his wound could not do much else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you describe him as a fighter?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he might have had some sort of army-style trousers or something of -- on. Perhaps he had been able to -- he was a wounded man, you know. He had a -- he had a problem that -- to me it was obvious that, in fact, he couldn't do much else. But he was able to man the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, just on this issue which we touched on earlier about, your evidence was that you would have difficulty even describing the men of Srebrenica as fighters even. You said it wasn't an army. I want to ask you simply a few questions just about Naser Oric. And as a preliminary, you told us yesterday your mission was to assess the wounded and you didn't pay much attention to name. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you attend meetings of those involved in the defence of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can remember being taken just once to a -- to a hotel there for a short meeting with some -- you know, with some people. I don't -- I didn't even make any notes or -- you know, there was no -- there was nothing of importance to me to emerge from it I think other than nothing to interfere with my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So it correct to say that you didn't -- well, I'll put it this way: Before going to Srebrenica, did you receive intelligence, briefings about the personalities in Srebrenica and who was doing what?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I would not have been aware or taken an interest in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us how on your way to Konjevic Polje from Sarajevo you don't recall hearing anything about Naser Oric. I want to ask you now: When you were in Srebrenica itself, do you recall ever seeing Naser Oric, firstly?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing him in Srebrenica, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And during that time when you were in Srebrenica, did you ever hear anything about Naser Oric that you recall?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when you went back to Konjevic Polje, do you recall -- sorry, I'll withdraw that question. I want to take it in sequence. In the whole time you were in Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje, do you recollect anyone telling you anything about Naser Oric and any role he might have in the enclave when you were there in March?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it may seem -- it may seem a foolish question, but do you know anything of what Naser Oric was up to in December of 1994?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Where were you in December 1994?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You weren't -- or were you monitoring the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. There is a reason why I asked those questions, but thank you. Now, dealing with your return to Konjevic Polje. Firstly, can you describe for us how you returned there?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a message through the radio link transmitted by UNHCR that the wounded from Konjevic Polje were going to be evacuated that day, and this is early in the morning, and that I should make my way there by a specific time, by 1.00 or 2.00 in the afternoon. And I asked if some people could, you know, be provided to escort me there. And I waited, but none came. So myself and the interpreter that I had found and taken and employed, we set off and retraced that -- broadly that route. We were -- there was some shelling on the road, so we stopped and sheltered in some remains of buildings and while -- wondering what to do and then the -- some men -- again, I would not call these soldiers. Some men joined us. I think they did have some rifles or some -- between them, but they were very slow, physically, not wanting to be slow. They physically couldn't keep up later with me, and I left them behind. They followed later -- they arrived much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And I'm going to refer now that D777, "Merry Christmas, Mr. Larry." And I think on page 182 that recounts your return to Konjevici. Do you recall where you encountered shelling, do you recall the place?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside Srebrenica before Potocari and there was -- we were fired at by machine-gun which I think was from a hill called Caus, C-a-u-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if I might lead a little on just his return to Konjevic Polje if it's not in dispute. It's simply to make progress about what this witness saw on his return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Jones. And the understanding is as usual: If Mr. Di Fazio stands up and objects, then we take the objection and we decide. Otherwise, unless I hear any objections from the Prosecution, please continue leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I think I can do it by simply reading a passage from this book. It's page 182, and it's referring to you stepping out at our own pace after you've left these others behind. "He knew he was on the right track when he hit a wall of refugees, fleeing Konjevici. They helped his map reading but hindered his pace. He forced his way through family group after family group, all struggling in the deep snow, carrying babies, holding on to toddlers, dragging bundles." So pausing there, isn't it right that you had hit a stream of refugees, families, toddlers leaving Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. They didn't physically hold me up, but it was quite obvious it was easy to find the way to go from them. And many of them were crying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was a pretty miserable sight?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now it goes on there in the book to describe how with the last 15 minutes for -- to meet a deadline you managed to purchase a bicycle and cycled into Konjevici. Then it says: "Near the centre of Konjevici he almost collided with Naser Oric. 'Have you seen UNPROFOR?' he asked him. "Oric knew everything that went on, but he pretended not to understand. 'UNPROFOR?' 'Yes. Have they left? 'They left the day after you arrived.' Simon did not have time to waste amusing Oric. He pedaled on to the municipal buildings." Stopping there, do you think that's a fair comment about your encounter with Naser Oric upon your return?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the author has used a lot of poetic license because I don't agree with those sentiments. I don't recall them, and I don't know how else he could have thought that -- how else he could have reported them. But I did -- but I did -- I do believe I met him, I'm sure it was him, pretty sure, it was him that I met. I can't say for absolute sure, but I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And while we're on the subject I want to deal just with a couple of other references to Oric in this book. Do you have it in front of you? All right. It's page 175.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you still -- yes, we are still in chapter 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. D777.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's the last paragraph on page 175. And this is -- I'm taking this out of chronological sequence, but I'm dealing with these references to Oric in the book. "There were two main locations of the sick and a number of houses where one or two were billeted. Naser Oric had told the General that there were seven hundred who needed evacuating. We did not see many more than a couple hundred in total. Maths was not Oric's strong suit. We reckoned that seventy needed urgent treatment." Can you comment on that, whether that's a fair comment?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with this. There were -- there were a larger number of locations then is implied here. I received -- I can't remember how, but I had received some indication of the work that the team had done while I was in Srebrenica, that they had assessed 76 patients. Over the following day I counted a lot more than that, but they would have been fresh -- more freshly wounded. And a very important point is that people here were counting houses where people were receiving treatment. As soon as they were able to get out of what was a makeshift ward, hospital ward in a room or in a house or in a restaurant, they were -- you know, they would have gone -- their families would have then looked after them. And those larger number of people also fulfil criteria for medical evacuation in these conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's helpful. And then -- and finally, and obviously we won't -- I'm not seeking to be overly critical of Larry Hollingworth, but just to clarify some of these references. You told us how you weren't in fact particularly interested in following the -- any sort of military situation. If we turn to page 173, it's at the top, and this is describing the entry into Konjevic Polje and it refers to the men at the barricade at this tree. It says: "They were tired, tetchy, and nervous. 'You cannot do anything until we have spoken to the commander,' they said. This made sense. Their commander is Naser Oric, a tough leader who rules with a rod of iron." Now, firstly do you recall any conversation along the lines of: Take me to see Commander Oric, as it appears in the next sentence, or any reference to Oric at that stage?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But then it would not have been my job to get involved with a discussion. I would have stayed in or next to the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So it's simply this: Where it's stated that Oric is a tough leader who rules with a rod of iron, that's not something over which you can comment on one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I think finally there's a reference to Oric sending a car to meet you. Is that -- is that something which is accurately reported here to your knowledge? I'll find the reference in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Halfway down page 173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "Naser Oric sent a vehicle to pick up the General. The rest of us struggled for hours forcing a gap wide enough to let our vehicles to pass."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that something which you recollect?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that General Morillon might have got through and ahead and -- and, you know, started meeting while the rest of us stayed with the vehicles until -- until the vehicles could go -- could pass. I can't comment any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall offhand - and without referring to your notes of course on this very subject - but if there's anything else you felt you needed to correct in this chapter?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To quite a lot of minor things, I don't think of any consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine, if they're not of any consequence. Right. Now, I want to deal with a couple of further matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I am conscious of the time and what I might propose at some stage is to tender a number of exhibits without dwelling excessively on them, but I have prepared a number of exhibits for this witness which we want on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, earlier you gave evidence about this road convoy which arrived in Tuzla. And I would just ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, it's already an exhibit it's D680.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But I need you to have a look at that to confirm whether or not you're the author. D680, please. Do you recall this report and are you the author?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think that's -- I think that's all which is necessary for this exhibit. I simply wanted to confirm that. And then there's another exhibit, a new exhibit, which is a monthly report of WHO Sarajevo office, 14th March to 15th April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, out of an abundance of caution, since this is a WHO report, I would rather have it -- your tendering to be recorded, at least temporarily, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, Your Honour. I might just ask one question of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that actually it is a project of WHO to put its documents in the public domain?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was contacted many years ago about assisting -- I was told of the -- yes, a project to assemble all documents for -- for a permanent record of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We will keep it under seal, but just to mention that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the day it does mention persons, if you look at page 2, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think the safest way is to have it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become D78 -- I have lost track, Madam Registrar. 786?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D786, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D786, and it will be temporarily under seal. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to take you to page 4, and it's the second paragraph. And there that paragraph relates to Srebrenica. And I read: "Problems included epidemic diarrhoea, scabies and lice infestation, poor water and food supplies, and the absence of effective local organisation." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And it's actually that the phrase I want to draw your attention to: "The absence of effective local organisation." Now, that's something you commented on earlier. Can you comment in relation to -- to that phrase and what you understood that to refer to?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a recurring report and impression from anyone, including myself, there that the local organisation was not sufficiently -- was not sufficient to deal with the continually deteriorating conditions and the continually increasing numbers of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: With respect to this evidence, firstly for it to be understood I think the witness has to specify what sort of organisation he is referring to. It may be the witness is referring to the local organisation of medical facilities in the hospital and so on, rather than any other sort of local organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And it's important for that to be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's a very fair comment, Mr. Di Fazio. Perhaps, Mr. Jones, could you address this distinction that Mr. Di Fazio is eliciting from your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you understand this reference to effective local organisation to be confined to the hospital and the medical system or to apply more broadly?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's applied more broadly to all matters concerning the support of community or any managing of community, whether it was crowd control around -- around evacuation of wounded or vulnerable groups on buses or lorries or whether it was addressing water -- trying to improve water supply or food distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then further down on the same page, the last paragraph: "Many of the personnel working in the enclaves," and I'll avoid mentioning the names of the agencies, "have witnessed awful scenes. This particular blend of violence, disorder, and helplessness, makes post-traumatic stress more likely."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, if you're able to comment what you in Tuzla -- or, sorry, what you would understand in that report, what that would refer to.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combination of deteriorating public health conditions, the large numbers of wounded, that tragedies like the schoolyard shelling and the conditions that they're working in of -- with, for example, poor lighting, unsafe from shelling, and the despair and the difficulty in resting while in the enclave, combined -- there are a large number there of the established risk factors for later development of post-traumatic stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You've referred to this schoolyard shelling. I'm going to tender some exhibits in that regard in a moment. I have one more exhibit on this subject, though, and it's, again, I suppose under seal and, in an abundance of precaution, since it's addressed to WHO Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm saying out of an abundance of precaution because from past experience, particularly the way you haven't heard beforehand from these international organisations, they come afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it's easier if we have taken this precaution before rather than have to deal with it when these documents would have already been made available --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely endorse the Court's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you understand I'm not trying to keep them out of the records capriciously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all. I entirely agree Your Honour's with that approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you could confirm that this was indeed authored by you, as it appears? And you need to answer verbally.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, myself and a colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, the date is the 22nd of April, 1993. We see there, and this is a report from someone who had been in Srebrenica: "Massive overcrowding, diarrhoea still a problem, filthy living conditions for displaced people, difficulty of lice, scabies, et cetera, and prevent reinfection." My question is this: This was after demilitarisation of April 1993, is it correct that these problems you've testified about continued even after demilitarisation, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to my knowledge they appeared to continually deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this document that the witness has just testified about is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit 787, and it will enter into the record under seal for the time being until further order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, on the matter which you referred to of the schoolyard shelling, there are a couple of exhibits which I would like to pass up. There's one which is a telex dated 12th of April, 1993. The subject is: "Slaughter of civilians in Srebrenica." And I'm going to avoid, yes, referring to the persons whose name is mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It refers to sit reps which describe: "Appalling casualties from shelling of the densely packed town of Srebrenica. In his early reports, he is forced to use the phrase after a day of terror and horror we are only guess to the scenes later which have led to a total of 56 dead and 73 seriously wounded. Their little surgical team will have been overwhelmed by this number of casualties, and many more can be expected to die. It appears that even the long and difficult retreat to the south is blocked, therefore the people are completely trapped by advancing frontlines. Their main water supply from higher up the valley has previously been cut off. With a population of around 60.000, many of whom displaced from what has previously been acknowledged as ethnic cleansing, then the present situation can only be described as an impending holocaust." Now, by question for you regarding this exhibit is, you spoke earlier of the very difficult conditions under which the people in Srebrenica had to operate. Here you refer to an impending holocaust. Is that an opinion which you would endorse?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a very -- it's a very strong and emotive term and not one that people would usually use, but in this case I felt it appropriate. I've never -- I would never have used that term before or since to any other situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this document that the witness has asked about is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit 778, and it is being entered into the records temporarily under seal until further order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There is now less information publicising the events that are occurring in Srebrenica. We owe it to the people in that town and to the international staff working there to use all means possible to help them. I believe we also owe it to the Serbian people to reveal the reality of the situation, if they and their children are to be spared the dignity and shame that would eventually follow any genocide perpetrated by their leaders."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, is that right, then, that you considered there was a risk of genocide back in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the people of Srebrenica, the people who you saw and spoke with when you were there in March 1993, in your opinion, were they fearing the same -- did they share these fears of an impending holocaust?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. Specifically I remember, for example, ordinary families saying they could cope with the fear of Bosnian Serb army from their neighbouring region and towns that they had lived in and -- but they were particularly frightened of armed forces, Bosnian Serb forces from outside of their region who did not have any -- who would not show any sympathy or respect to them in the event that the -- in the event that the -- they were overrun, the enclave was overrun.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've described how just malnutrition could lead to people neglecting basic duties of life, for example, hygiene. In your opinion, living with that prospect, did that affect the priorities of the people living in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could you be more specific? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can give an example. Would people have been concerned to investigate if there had been possible vandalism to Serb property in that time, or would they be more concerned to avoid this holocaust?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Preoccupation was survival of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have another exhibit which, again, I think the same procedure should be adopted as previously. It's a -- I believe it's a telex which has been -- I'll ask this witness, but I believe it was printed off in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Eventually, Mr. Jones and Mr. Di Fazio, if you come to the conclusion that you need to give publicity to these documents, the way I see it, there can be redactions of names and other matters and it could be done that way. But for the time being I think we need to continue adopting this precautionary approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Mardel, looking at that document, are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact we can see in fact at the top -- well, I won't mention the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me proceed to the substance of it. We can all see from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime before you do so, let me record this -- the entry of this document, please. The witness is about to testify on -- about a document consisting of four pages. You are alleging that he prepared this document himself, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not prepared, no; that he printed it off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That he printed it off. Okay. This document is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit 789. For the reasons I mentioned earlier on, it is being entered into the records under seal for the time being until further orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Mardel, firstly is it right that you received this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communication came directly on to my machine in my office and I took a copy of it while handing it to the addressee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. You forwarded it to other agencies?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, across the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just want to turn to page 3. I'm going to read two passages. First: "The stress and danger level in Srebrenica is such that all personnel should be rotated after a maximum of two weeks. People in the pocket witness unimaginable horrors and come close to losing their own lives when carrying out everyday activities." Then I move down to where he starts to describe events of 12th April, 1993. "Although I had witnessed many terrible scenes in Srebrenica, primarily of civilians being blown apart by shelling, nothing I have ever seen compares to 12 April 1993 in terms of sheer horror." Then further on down he says, the author of this document: "I will never be able to convey the sheer horror and the atrocity I witnessed on April 12th." Then he goes on,- further on to say: "A second round of shelling into Srebrenica took place between 1550 and 1610, resulting in further casualties. I saw the top of one house blown off less than 50 metres from my position while travelling with UNMOs in their GMC." Now, firstly I wanted to deal with that reference to rotation after two weeks. Would you be able to confirm that for the people in Srebrenica who experienced these shellings and these horrors, that they must have been severely traumatised?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We've seen the reference of the horrors of shelling in terms of loss of human life. In this trial we are concerned with the damage to property which shelling can cause. We saw this reference: "I saw the top of one house blown off less than 50 metres from my position." On the basis of your experience when you were in the pocket, can you confirm that Serb shelling could rip off roofs and cause serious damage to property?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the heavier shelling meant that a house was not -- was no longer safe. You could be killed in spite of sheltering indoors.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think that's enough for this document. I'm trying to finish before the break and I think I might be able to sneak in before the break. There is another exhibit which I want to pass up which, for different reasons, I was going to ask to keep under seal. And it's at the request of this witness, for reasons of which, if necessary can be explained in closed session if the Prosecution objects to it being kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll do it differently. We'll have it entered into the record, temporarily under seal, not to lose time, Mr. Jones. Then you discuss amongst yourselves and if it's the case of reviewing or going back on that decision, we will do it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. This will be Defence Exhibit 790 in the meantime, and it is being entered into the records temporarily under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And, Dr. Mardel, are you happy for us to address this document in public session?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the only document that I would ask if it could not be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Let's go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have two finally matters I think I can deal with very shortly. The first is actually from the Hollingworth book which is an exhibit -- has previously been entered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that you read from if it's not too lengthy a quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This concerns a press conference, following the shelling of the schoolyard, attended by yourself and Larry Hollingworth: "Simon Mardel and I attended the press conference in Sarajevo the following morning. I made the following statement. 'Simon and I wish to speak, as we have shared some of the anguish of the people of Srebrenica. When yesterday I heard the news about the shelling, my first thought was of the army commander who ordered the shelling. I hope that he burns in the hottest part of hell." Do you recall that press conference?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then further down on that page ti says, and this is still Larry Hollingworth speaking: "'I then thought about my Serb friends whom I have met on my travels. Do they wish to read in future history books that their army has chased innocent women and children from village to village until they are finally cornered in Srebrenica, a place from which there is no escape, and where their fate is to be transported like cattle or slaughtered like lambs." And what I want to ask you about that is, you referred earlier to the people of Srebrenica having been chased to the last refuge. Is that something which you -- is that your considered opinion, that they were against the well, as it were?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I was aware of both the geographical -- because of the loop of the river Drina as well as the political and military sort of front -- you know, front line. So there was no other option of safety for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally, is it right that you were awarded Order of the British Empire, OBE, for your service?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Di Fazio, do you think that 45 minutes will be enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, so I'm going to ask that we have a shorter break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I suggest the following: We will have a shorter break, 25 minutes instead of 30. And do -- can I count on the cooperation of all the staff, interpreters, et cetera, to then stay over for maybe five minutes, maximum ten minutes more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think if we do that I should -- should -- I mean, it's possible that I'll finish even earlier than the 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I should be able to finish in that time. What I'm concerned about is if you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but anyway. Okay. All right. Let's have a shorter break, 25 minutes, please. And everyone, please try to be as punctual as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I -- my apologies, but in my haste there were two photographs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to point that out the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would be grateful if they could be exhibited because the witness did say that he took them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the last two photos in the bundle that was handed over earlier, the photo which includes the three children in the foreground is being marked as Defence Exhibit D791. And the other photo which shows two men and two women is being marked as Exhibit D792. Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Dr. Mardel, I just want to ask you very briefly about the first night after your arrival in Konjevic Polje. You'd got in I think late on the night of the 5th, had this meeting with what you saw as representatives, and then circumstances presented themselves such that you could do the hike into Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. Was a gentleman named Pyers Tucker with you on that night?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I now know the name, but then I wasn't aware of who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure. Were there other soldiers about whose names you didn't know accompanying your party?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew most of them, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just bear with me a moment. Could the witness be shown D224, and to save extra trips, D232 might as well be taken up to the witness as well, please. Oh, and D777, sorry. And they can be kept there for the duration of my cross-examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one are you going to start --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one are you going to start with?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Exhibit D224, which is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So perhaps, I suppose, we ought to go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends on what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, perhaps I can save us the trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends. It's doesn't necessarily follow that everything that is under seal, anything that has to do with it has to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You can find out who the author of this document is, Dr. Mardel, if you go to the second page, and you see at the top, it says H -- it says various things. And then on -- there's a little -- couple of boxes, and you can see there's a reference to who drafted the document.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. Okay, and then if you turn over the next page, you go to -- you refer to Konjevic Polje, and there's a reference to General -- General Morillon visiting a certain place at a certain time on a certain date. You see the date? Paragraph 4, directly underneath the heading "Konjevic Polje." It says: "The General ..." visited a certain place Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from 8.00 to 10.30 on a certain date.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And it then goes on to say that whilst the UN -- representative of an international body and another international body explored the village.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Larry Hollingworth the representative of one of those two bodies mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I don't think I can -- I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, fine.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's -- I won't press on with that. Have you got any reason -- well, let me put it -- ask you this: Do you agree that there was such a tour of Konjevic Polje by members of your party, as far as you know, because I know you weren't there, but as far as you know, was there such a tour the following day, on the 6th of March?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A tour of Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of -- to assess the wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I was somehow passed or received --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a list of the numbers of wounded and was then able to work from that list and see who was -- there was deaths or additions or movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. In fact, if you now look at D232, which we can openly refer to, that's your report.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And on the sixth page, that's three from the last page, you deal with the medical situation in Konjevic Polje. You refer to an assessment on the 6th of March.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Which was a -- medical in nature because you received a copy of a list of patients.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 76 patients. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Thank you. You have -- you can put the documents down. I have just finished with them for the moment. You referred to food boxes -- actually, no, if you could get D232 again, please. On the same page, there's a reference to food boxes, under the heading "Food Supplies."

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you counted only half the number of boxes that there should have been in this supermarket that you visited. Do you know what happened to the other half?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they were either not found or, more commonly, kept by people, understandably, in those conditions for their own families or selves, or eaten on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you actually see people eating the meals?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly saw a lot of the very distinctive wrappers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Wrappers, okay. But you actually don't know if a significant portion of that half that went missing was collected in an organised or formal way by any other body or group. You just couldn't say if that happened or if that did not happen?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but, you know, these are being dropped in rural areas in snow. The -- this was not seen as a particular problem, that only half were collected. What was -- what mattered was that they were out by a large factor of about four or five for the entire enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not with you. Out by what, sorry?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large fact -- the air drop had to be increased by about three times the total supply on the basis of -- of this estimation. Not -- you know, for 50 per cent loss of whatever it was not the real issue; there was just -- the total number was insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would never expect a scattered air drop to have anything like a full collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. There's going to be inevitable loss because of all sorts of factors, correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: One factor might be hungry, starving people stealing them as they arrived, drifted down out of the sky and hit the ground. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But you don't know if there was any other factor, such as some sort of formal or more organised appropriation of the food.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You don't. Thank you. You gave extensive evidence about the medical conditions that you observed, the horrific conditions that you observed in Srebrenica. And I don't need to -- I've heard all of that and I don't need to dwell on that. Is it the case that there were groupings within the Srebrenica area, the part of Srebrenica that you saw, the town and any other part that you saw on your way into Srebrenica and back to Konjevic Polje, who suffered more than others? And I'm referring to people who lived in the town and had been residents of the town, people who lived in villages just outside of the town, and people who were refugees who had been displaced from other more outlying areas and had come into the town. Bearing those three groupings in mind, would you say that the degree to which they suffered from all of the conditions that you described was more intense in the group of refugees who had come in from outlying areas to seek shelter and take refuge in Srebrenica? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The worst group would be internally displaced people who did not have relatives or friends to stay with and had no -- no means of getting good shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yeah. Right. And in fact I think there's actual reference in D232, your report, to that. You -- on the fourth page -- my copy is not numbered. On the fourth page, you say -- you refer to people -- three broad classes of people with different nutritional status. Of course, none of them were doing very well, of course, but people living in villages, they had, as you say, considerable advantages because of close-knit society, knowledge of the land, and so on. And then you describe your observations. And then over the page, there's a second grouping, people who own houses and who may -- in Srebrenica and who may have relatives in the nearby villages. And in fact, you refer to a -- in that second grouping, you refer to the town hall having a list of high-priority people who were said to be in greatest need. Now, were those high-priority people who were said to be in greatest need also people who were suffering the most from the physical afflictions that you've described; the malnutrition, the anaemia, the infection, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was -- it appeared -- there was obviously a compromise between who they had records of and how accessible they were to finding those people and also how they in turn had access to that stationary soup kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And there's no doubt about it when you deal with the third group, the displaced people, you say: "These refugees are the most vulnerable group as they fall outside the help offered by village or town communities." They are the group that exhibited, by far, the most symptoms of all of the afflictions that you have described in Court. Correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The point of this is vulnerability. I'm highlighting vulnerability. I know I've used the word "nutritional status," but we use food security as -- an evaluation of people's food security. So it's not necessarily the condition they're in right now, but how vulnerable they would be to continuing -- where effort needs to be targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is it the case that the greater access to food a person has, the more likely they are to be healthy than a person who has lesser access to food?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: A basic rule --

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would be very surprised if he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the displaced people were the ones having the most trouble getting access to food, weren't they, from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were especially vulnerable, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the conditions that you saw, and as far as you're aware, had been exacerbated or at least largely compounded by a more recent wave of refugees in January -- from -- starting at about January, February, who had flooded into Srebrenica. I mean January, February of 1993. Do -- is that what your information told you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew there were recent and I saw recent internally displaced people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure. I have no doubt you saw that. But did you have intelligence information to the effect that in January, February there had been a large influx of refugees into Srebrenica, refugees from the outlying areas?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember a specific date. I've -- I recall an impression that there was a continual top-up or continual increase in people. And if somewhere like Cerska fell, then there were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the time that you were there, were there any outbreaks of typhus?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was concerned about a potential for typhus and just reported the detailed accounts that could suggest that it was there, but, you know, I can't confirm it and I -- you know, I haven't -- I have nothing -- nothing to confirm that there was typhus and didn't see any cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Lice infestation. To an untrained observer looking at someone who was suffering from lice, is it the case that a person can suffer from degrees of lice infestation? So to the untrained observer looking on -- looking at someone, they may not see any real obvious sign of lice infestation, but in a very heavy infestation it would be manifest -- clearly visible to the naked eye?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
