utterances.text: There's three different kinds of lice. Clothing lice --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- are, you know, common. And you have to look -- they prefer to live in the seams of clothing --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so they are absolutely not visible to the untrained eye. Head lice are, if it's a heavy infestation, you may notice them close up, but sometimes people can even not appreciate that someone -- a patient they're treating has them and then you're -- without looking very closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You've spoken about stressors and stress factors on people that were operating at the time. Is being incarcerated in a small, dank, dark room a stressful -- normally a quite stressful thing?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: A person who was suffering from lice infestation and may or may not -- and is suffering -- let me rephrase that. A person who was suffering from lice infestation and is also malnourished and is subjected to brutal and vicious assault using boots, gun butts, instruments such as pieces of wood, being punched on a fairly regular basis, is their ability to be able to withstand that physical assault greatly diminished by their condition, with the lice infestation and the malnutrition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lice infestation wouldn't affect their ability. It is a risk factor for typhus and typhus is endemic to that part of the world. It exists and it could have been a serious -- very lethal epidemic. Their nutritional status would affect their ability to heal from bruises or fractures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And would it affect their -- whether or not they succumbed to their injuries resulting from a savage assault, such that they are more likely to die than a person in good, robust health?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even severe anaemia would compromise your ability to heal from wounds that could otherwise be survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And malnutrition -- the onset of clinical malnutrition, what you would recognise and describe medically as malnutrition, does that depend on, I assume, how much food you're getting and the quality of the food? If it's really bad, I assume the onset is faster; if it's not so bad, I assume the onset is slower. Is that essentially correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's not just the quantity but the quality of the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. Okay. If food a person is receiving is bad in both terms of quality and quantity, over what period of time would you expect that person to develop symptoms of malnutrition that you as a doctor would say, yes, that person has got -- is suffering from malnutrition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends extraordinarily to a great extent on the balance of the nutrition. Some micronutrients or vitamins, you can get a deficiency occurring easily within a month. Vitamin C, folate, some vitamins are not stored in the body and need constant replenishment. The body -- people will cope with a couple of weeks of starvation quite -- quite well, but once you run into, you know, more prolonged periods -- but I have to emphasise, it depends on the nature. For example, Sarajevo, people require 600 grams of food a day to maintain nutritional status. There's even a formula for winter conditions when they burn more fuel. For that period that I was in Sarajevo, for much of that time the average portion actually arriving in Sarajevo per person and distributed was about 250. So they were, you know, malnourished but not -- they were able -- even that 50 per cent ration, or abouts, was sufficient to keep them going. But Srebrenica was a very different -- were totally different figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what sort of time periods can people survive for in the scenario that you just described where there's about a 50 per cent ration of what is necessary to keep a person alive?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will depend on how big you are to start with, what activities you're doing, the coldness of your surroundings and how much of your energy you need to convert to heat just to stay alive. So there's a huge number of factors. And as I said, the micronutrients, the vitamins, can actually play a large role. It's a slippery slope. People don't die, as such, of starvation. They die, for example, of pneumonia because their body can't produce antibodies. Antibodies are made of protein. You see people losing their muscle mass, that's protein, they also lose their antibody production, so they become prone to infections. So it's a complex balance of the environment and exposure and what particular bugs, bacterial viruses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Look, I don't even think I need to show you the photos. I'm actually looking at Exhibits D785 and D781, and one is the photograph of the poor gentleman obviously badly, badly emaciated, with a splint on his leg. You've told us about that.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And then you see by contrast the two gentlemen operating the radio --

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- in Exhibit D785. Now, to the untrained eye, of course, my untrained eye, the gentleman with the splint clearly appears to be suffering from starvation or malnutrition, whereas the other two seem reasonably healthy. Would you -- did you see those sorts of contrasts? Firstly, do you accept my basic description of the men depicted in these photographs; and secondly, did you see contrasts like that in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a mistake to evaluate nutritional status just on a facial appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those young -- the young twins there, they've got thin faces, but most of the face is made up of bony structure. You would need to look at arm circumference, for example, to see how much protein they've lost, or fat and protein. So it's not a valid -- they're not valid comparisons. If we just look at the two faces, for example, that would be invalid, compare all their faces. The fact that that man has got his arms and part of his pelvis exposed gives us more of an ability. But, yes, he's in hospital and he's got a wound. There are clearly other contributing factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, thanks. Now, the gentlemen who took you over from Konjevic Polje to -- down to Srebrenica were obviously fit, young men, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And do you know who assigned them to help you -- to take you across the -- through those paths and eventually down to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who. It obviously was an assignation and it was -- there was organisation. They were clearly tasked to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. Now, for -- for a person who's been living in the Srebrenica area from about April of 1992 up until the time you arrived, in order for a man, youngish man, to be able to carry weaponry, possibly carry ammunition, to be able to march reasonably long distances through harsh terrain, uphill and down dale, over mountains, in the cold, and go into combat would require that person to have a certain degree of nourishment in order for him to be able to carry out that task. You would have to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And people suffering from malnutrition would be unable to do that, certainly on a -- on anything like a continuous basis. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The young men that you saw and who took you up over the hill and down into Srebrenica would have been quite capable, wouldn't they, of carrying weaponry, ammunition, travelling long distances, and going into action at the end of it?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you actually lay eyes on Mr. Oric when you were in Konjevic Polje? Do you have any --

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may well have done, but I can't remember that. The fact that I can't remember that doesn't mean that I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the time that you were in Srebrenica, did you -- were you made aware of any body called a War Presidency that was overseeing local -- a local authority called the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I go back to your previous question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have misunderstood you. Are you referring to did I see Mr. Oric at the meeting in what was reported as the school room on my way in, or did I meet him at any stage? Because I believe I did meet him on my way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, yes, actually --

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did meet him on my way out, if I may clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you've got no memory of meeting him on the way in?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But you do recall seeing him or meeting him on the way out?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And did he strike you as being a fit, powerful, young man?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I wouldn't have -- there's no reason I could have made an assessment if -- as I recall the meeting, people were standing by the road. I asked questions, I asked for water, and, you know, I -- it was a station -- they directed me to where I could find the radio so I could communicate again --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with my organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just while we're on that, you mentioned when you were talking about D785, which is the photograph of the two young men next to the -- next to the radio set, that it was the - and I quote your words - "the only link with the outside world." Would I be correct in saying that it's the only link with the outside world that you saw? Or do you have any other information as to the existence of other radio sets?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before we continue because it appears to me, please, this last part of the witness's testimony as to the regards of what is the practice of his organisation, let's redact it, please. I don't think it is in the interests of anyone to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. In the meantime our registrar will look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: D777. And Mr. Hollingworth says this, he's talking about a period of time when presumably you had gone down to Srebrenica. "He arranged for Lawrence and myself to go to the amateur radio station which was in a small house on the top of a hill. The living-room was comfortably furnished. Along one wall was a desk and on the desk was the 'ham' radio where a young man in uniform sat. 'I want to speak to Simon in Srebrenica. Is he there yet?' 'Oh yes, he got there early this morning. He is in the hospital now.'" So from --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And then the -- and then eventually contact is established. So do you have any memory of being contacted from Konjevic Polje in Srebrenica through the use of radio sets?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I may have to think hard about that. I don't recall a -- it's possible that Mr. Hollingworth may have spoken to me, but quite often there were, kind of, messages left or we knew there'd been contact made. And I -- I only recall the contacts with -- with Tuzla and a UNHCR representative by the radio there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But you're not, I take it, ruling out such a matter?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It could have happened that you've got no memory of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be fair to the witness, in that extract, it's a reference for a message being left for the visitor, not to contact -- being established two-way contact. So that's what's being referred to in this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You don't have any memory of receiving a message that apparently had been left for you by way of radio in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- I think I did receive messages, but most of them were from -- were from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. Now, let's just get back to the civil authorities. I was asking you about a War Presidency. Did you ever become aware of the existence of any such body in the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of a War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Of something called a War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I would not -- my job would not -- it's not in the nature of my job, you know, to know or find out of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand that perfectly well. I understand what your brief was and what you were there to do. What you say makes perfect sense, with respect. But I will continue to ask you nonetheless, because you may have learned from other sources. Were you aware or did you see anything that indicated the existence of a military police in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you aware of or see anything that indicated to you the existence of a staff command for fighters in Srebrenica, a command headquarters of some sort, some description?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a map -- one map on a wall in a room that I looked at and was shown in discussions about how I would go back to Konjevic Polje. And the -- you know, the -- that was not a civilian kind of a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or the -- you know, and when asking for an escort, which I -- which never kind of materialised every day except on the last day after I left, I must have been asking someone with -- with -- with some access to getting me an escort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that that answers your question, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. Well, not entirely, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is the map -- I asked you about the existence of a -- of a staff command or a command headquarters, and you took us to this issue of the map.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you -- in your mind do you associate the existence of a map with a staff command or is -- are you just saying that because it's the only thing you can offer in terms of seeing anything that might indicate --

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my only experience. I know the hotel -- there was a brief meeting in the hotel, you know, that -- you know, that may have been some sort of structure linked to that building. But this map was either in the radio room or in a building or in the same building or nearby. And I reported to that room every day ready to go with my rucksack and belongings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. You've mentioned a hotel. Are you saying that the map was in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, completely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you become aware of a place called a PTT building, is it like the postal or telegraph building in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I later found that they were referring to the radio room as that, and I -- in retrospect I think there was -- sort of a telephone building --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But to me it was a radio -- the room where the map was and where I would go was either to an adjacent building or the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be absolutely clear on that. The building that you've described as the sort of telephone building, is that the building where you saw this map of which you have been speaking? If you can't remember --

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that with a hundred per cent --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they must have been fairly close proximity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Thanks for your help. Just one last thing. D232, which I think you have there, is talking about Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic. And Mr. Jones took you to the passage where you speak of him, and he took you to the reference to Dr. Mujkanovic having the appearance of being burnt out. And in your report you go on to say: "Now spends much of his time attending other matters in the town." Do you know what other matters he was attending to?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know if they were civilian, humanitarian, organisational matters. The other doctors adjusted their clinicals, they didn't deal with the sort of wider issues and they didn't deal with any trauma surgery, for example. So I was aware -- I felt that he -- he didn't want -- he wanted to avoid doing too much work anymore, and that was the point of making that, that he, you know, was -- was trying to find other responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I could completely understand that, and I was trying to say that tactfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, that wasn't actually my last topic, just one more. Hollingworth, Larry Hollingworth, did you see him down in Srebrenica in those five days or so that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So he -- do you know where he was in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must have spent -- well, he wasn't -- you know, they left Konjevic Polje, you know, the following day after I -- I'd left or shortly after. I assume they would have gone back to Tuzla or Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you see him in later weeks and month?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you help him write his book or contribute to it?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me to contribute -- for details, much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you have any idea or knowledge if he spent much time with Mr. Oric, Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: His position in his organisation, he would deal with figures of authority or people, you know, people in a community and would be more -- is likely to have met a great number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Dr. Mardel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Jones, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, only a very few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In cross-examination a scenario was put to you where someone had been a victim of a vicious and brutal assault and there were the other contributory factors that could lead to illness or death. In the course of your examination-in-chief, we spoke about multifactorial factors of death. My question is this: If someone is malnourished, is suffering from disease and also suffers an assault, never mind whether it's a brutal and vicious assault, an assault, isn't it not a matter of a question of degree as to what is the substantial cause of death if someone dies who is malnourished, who has been beaten and who has -- suffers from disease?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Different degrees of trauma we would, for example, see in the elderly, a small amount of trauma can result in death because of contributing factors of delayed wound healing, inability to stop bleeding themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how, in fact, in the UK do you deal with that if you have to fill in a death certificate when recording the cause of death where there are many causes?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our country we have three separate sections of cause of death. So you can have cause of death in itself, antistent [phoen] cause, and then a third one, what even might have caused that, and then there's another section of contributing factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you may not plunk for a particular, substantial cause of death; it may be several factors which all caused death?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a hierarchy. There is prior cause of death and then factors which influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were asked -- looking at two of the photographs, about what you can tell by looking at them. I just want very quickly to show you one of the photographs which you didn't deal with, D791, and it's again to comment on what one can tell from appearances. I don't know if you have the photographs with you still. It's the one with the three children in the front. Sorry, D791. It's simply to ask you this: In this picture I think you would agree none of the people are smiling at all, are they, in this family picture?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that usual? Is that -- is there anything which you would draw from that -- from those appearances?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they're demoralised and frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In your experience in taking photographs in war zones, how common is it to have a picture like that where in fact nobody is even trying a smile?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's unusual. People are relieved to see someone from the outside, to see someone -- you know, to see signs of support. And whilst they are very appreciative of me, I think circumstances -- their circumstances were too severe to -- to do -- to give the normal, automatic response to a camera, worldwide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you were asked about civil authorities in Srebrenica, and I think you said you weren't aware of any. In Konjevic Polje were you aware of a mayor or any type of civil authority?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I thought that there was -- I don't know if it's the right word, but there was a woman who was, you know, leading the community. I referred to her as mayor or she was referred to -- I don't know if that's my misreading of her status, but she had a responsibility for the community and sometimes spoke for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked about a command headquarters and you referred to this map. Would you accept that a map -- a map on a wall isn't indicative or doesn't prove that there is a structure or staff command? You weren't saying that, actually, were you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it was, you know, the thing that stuck in my mind as a, you know, as a point that I went to about leaving the pocket each day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And that map would have dated from before the conflict I take it?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it was a proper, printed, colour map, yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In other words, it hadn't been produced in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if the witness can talk about when the map was produced or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the objection has to be sustained, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's an invitation to a world of speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's use the least time possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are already over the time limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Just two points. Firstly, the witness answered "no" to my question. Secondly, it's not speculative if I ask the witness, Did you see any facilities, did anyone indicate to you that it was possible to publish a coloured map in Srebrenica at that time.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to regularly in Sarajevo go to the map-producing room and I could see the complexity of that to produce black and white, large black and white maps which had the red lines in -- red ink was the only colour, outlining the areas which we had to be aware of. So that's very sophisticated. I saw nothing -- really couldn't -- wouldn't have thought that anything like that would exist there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now -- two final questions. You referred to a hotel and you said: That may have been some sort of -- there may have been some sort of structure linked to that building. That's not something which you actually know one way or another, is it, whether there was some sort of organised military structure linked to a hotel, is it?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I was clearly taken to a meeting there, but I can't remember details from it and it didn't have any bearing on my reports. So I didn't put it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. You did say also that you reported to this room with the map. Had actually anyone told you to appear there on a daily basis or do you just mean that you showed up there?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was to have only stayed a day in Srebrenica, and so every day I was, you know, making a plan to leave. And I went there to get, you know, an escort to take me -- to take me out. But I spent a lot of time waiting there and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to make progress and to bring this to an -- no one told you, did they, to report to that location every day? That was our own initiative?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something must have made me, you know, pick that place to go to knowing that, you know, I'm going -- you know, I'm going to be given, you know, an escort to take me -- to guide me out of the pocket. But I can't remember what.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And absolutely finally, the last question which was put by my learned friend I don't believe you actually answered. It was: "Q. Do you have any idea or knowledge if he, Hollingworth, spent much time with Mr. Oric, Naser Oric?" And you gave an answer which was to do with Mr. Hollingworth meeting a great number of people. Do you have specific knowledge that Larry Hollingworth spent time with Naser Oric? And I would appreciate if you could answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Mr. Jones. There's one question from Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Doctor, during your stay at the hospital, did you notice that that was an armed person outside the entrance to this hospital?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I would have remembered if there had been. It was a very slippery, icy slope leading up to the entrance and it's cold. To have someone standing outside, I think I would have remembered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Do you, by the way, remember if a crowd was outside, a crowd of relatives of somebody brought in wounded to the hospital? Was there a sort of chaos around the hospital when you were there?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were clinics associated with it, so people, you know, large numbers of people attending. And people would have brought food for their sick relatives, so there would have been a more-than-usual number of people in and around a building like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser. It will soon be over, doctor. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Doctor, during the examination-in-chief you had been asked about the time when you were in Srebrenica, did you ever hear anything about Naser Oric that you recall? And your answer was: "Nothing that I recall." Now, what I want to know is that: Did you not recall the Naser Oric, that you haven't heard of him at all, or was it that you knew that there was a person like Naser Oric but you did not hear anything about him, what his duties are?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about a figurehead or -- or an individual, you know, that made any impression on me to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But that's not completely an answer to my question. Did you hear the name of Naser Oric at all?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite -- it's quite possible that I did. I don't -- I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, apart from Dr. Mujkanovic, whom you had mentioned, and other medical personnel, did you hear of any other people with whom they had to do their time? Did you hear the name of -- got the name of other people?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- you know, there were no key figures that I -- that I acknowledged or remembered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And with regard to your own function, would it have been important for you to know the name or function of those who had to do with General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: SIMON MARDEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who had to do with General Morillon? No. I was -- I was allowed to function, you know, freely, and so I didn't need to negotiate with anyone about what I could or couldn't do. The only points of reference daily were -- I wanted to use the radio and spent some time there. And every day I was ready to go back to Konjevic Polje, as was in the original plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser, and I thank you, Judge Brydensholt. I don't have questions for you, Dr. Mardel. I wish to express my gratitude on behalf of Chamber on your accepting to come over as a witness in this trial. And you will receive all the assistance that you require to facilitate your return back to your home or duties at the earliest. I wish to thank publicly both parties, Prosecution, for their cooperation, without which you would have had to return Monday. And also the technical staff, interpreters, court recorders, everyone else, for having overstayed like many -- on many other occasions here to make this possible. I also wish you on behalf of everyone present here a safe journey back home. Thank you. Now, before we rise, you have handed, Mr. Jones, a list of the documents that you would like to be forensically examined. I suppose you have a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. There is some of them, there are some of them, that are documents that have not been tendered into evidence, that they belong to the Prosecution, for which the registrar, as such, for the time being is not responsible. You can escort the witness out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like you -- because I don't want to keep anyone here for any longer, I would like to have an exchange among -- between you to see if you could agree on a protocol with regard to those documents, the documents that belong to the Prosecution, and come back to us on Monday morning if there is agreement. If there is no agreement, of course you will tell us that much. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of October, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.55 p.m.,
